paragraphs.source_en: “Ah, now this was a serious problem. My wife had made a request, one of the very few she makes in a whole year, and I was sincerely eager to grant it. Ordinarily I do nothing but scold her, refuse to speak to her, burden her with household worries, and leave the children in her care, and I have never once repaid her for all the labor of keeping the house. Today, by good fortune, I had some free time, and in my purse there happened to be that vulgar stuff, four or five one-yen notes, so I was quite able to take her. Besides, my wife wanted to go, and I wanted to take her. Yet however much I wanted to take her, with chills shaking my whole body and sparks dancing before my eyes, I could not possibly ride a streetcar; I could not even get as far as the place by the door where one puts on shoes. The more I thought, ‘Ah, how terribly sorry I am for her,’ the more the chills came over me and the darker my eyes grew. I thought that if I could quickly have the doctor look at me and take some medicine, I would probably be well again before four o’clock. So I consulted with my wife and sent someone to fetch Dr. Amaki, but unfortunately he had been on duty the night before and had not yet returned home. The message that came back was: ‘He will return at two in the afternoon, and as soon as he does, he will come to your house at once.’ What a nuisance! If only I could take some almond water now, I was certain to recover before four. But when one’s luck is bad, nothing goes as one wishes; this time I had hoped, for once, to see my wife’s smiling face and enjoy myself too. I had not expected that plan to fall through so suddenly. My wife, with a resentful expression, asked, ‘Can we really not go?’ I said, ‘We will go, certainly we will. By four o’clock I am sure this illness of mine will be gone. Don’t worry; hurry and wash your face or change your clothes, and wait for me.’ Though I said this with my mouth, my heart was filled with boundless emotion. The chills grew more and more violent, and my eyes grew darker and more unsteady. If I did not recover before four o’clock and could not keep my promise, there was no telling what a narrow-minded woman might do. What would I do if matters came to a pitiful and tragic pass? Thinking of what might happen if I met with some calamity, I felt I ought now to explain to her the principle that all conditioned things change and all who live must perish, so that if the worst occurred she would not be wholly unprepared in mind. I thought this might perhaps be a husband’s duty toward his wife. So I immediately called her into the study. I asked her, ‘Though you are a woman, surely you know at least the Western proverb that many a slip may occur between the cup and the lip?’ The moment my wife heard this, she flew into a rage. She said furiously, ‘Who is supposed to understand that crabbed foreign writing? You know perfectly well that I do not understand English, yet you deliberately use English to make fun of me. Very well, suit yourself; after all, I am someone who does not understand English. If you are so fond of English, why did you not marry some young woman graduated from a mission school? There is no one in the world as cold-hearted and faithless as you.’ Thus my original well-intentioned plan was broken off halfway. I must declare to you all that there was not the least malice in my use of English; it arose entirely from the deepest affection for my wife, and if it is interpreted as my wife interpreted it, I have no standing at all.
